posts.hook: Your API can be slow while its CPU looks almost idle.

posts.title: Pagination Without Surprises / Bottleneck Roadmap
posts.headline: Pagination Without Surprises
posts.hook: Page two can repeat or skip records even when every query succeeds.
posts.premise: Consider a changing feed ordered by creation time. Define a stable tie-breaker and whether the client needs a snapshot or a best-effort live view.
posts.takeaway: A cursor is an ordering contract, not just an encoded page number.
posts.question: Which bottleneck would you measure first?

rows.title: Specify the order
rows.detail: Sort by a deterministic tuple such as creation time and immutable ID, not by a nonunique timestamp alone.

rows.title: Bound the page
rows.detail: Enforce a server-side page-size limit and return only the fields required by the client.

rows.title: Choose the cursor
rows.detail: Encode the last ordering tuple and relevant filters; validate it instead of trusting arbitrary client SQL.

rows.title: Match the index
rows.detail: Use an index aligned with the filter and ordering tuple, then inspect the plan with realistic data.

rows.title: Define change semantics
rows.detail: Document what concurrent inserts, edits, and deletions mean for records between successive pages.

rows.title: Test the boundary
rows.detail: Exercise equal timestamps, deleted cursor rows, empty pages, and forward traversal through a large dataset.

rows.title: Offset pagination
rows.detail: Use offsets for small or mostly static lists where jumping to a page number is a genuine requirement.

rows.title: Trade-off / Offset pagination
rows.detail: Large offsets can scan discarded rows, and concurrent inserts can shift page boundaries.

rows.title: Keyset pagination
rows.detail: Use keyset traversal for large ordered feeds with a stable cursor and no requirement for arbitrary page jumps.

rows.title: Trade-off / Keyset pagination
rows.detail: Changing sort keys and reverse traversal require deliberate semantics rather than a token-shaped workaround.

rows.title: Snapshot results
rows.detail: Use a snapshot when exports or audits require a consistent view across all pages.

rows.title: Trade-off / Snapshot results
rows.detail: Snapshot lifetime, storage, and expiry become operational costs that need limits.

posts.title: File Uploads Without API Overload / Bottleneck Roadmap
posts.headline: File Uploads Without API Overload
posts.hook: Large uploads can exhaust your API before ordinary requests become expensive.
posts.premise: Separate upload authorization, byte transfer, and file processing. A stored object is not automatically a trusted or published document.
posts.takeaway: Uploading bytes, validating content, and publishing a file are different trust boundaries.
posts.question: Which bottleneck would you measure first?

rows.title: Authorize the upload
rows.detail: Check tenant ownership, allowed purpose, file limits, and the intended object namespace.

rows.title: Use bounded transfer
rows.detail: Choose a streamed API path or a short-lived scoped upload URL instead of buffering arbitrary files in memory.

rows.title: Validate completion
rows.detail: Confirm expected size and metadata using authoritative storage state, not a client success claim.

rows.title: Quarantine content
rows.detail: Keep untrusted files separate until required validation and defensive scanning complete.

rows.title: Process as a job
rows.detail: Run conversion or indexing asynchronously with resource limits and retry-safe outputs.

rows.title: Clean abandoned objects
rows.detail: Expire incomplete uploads and orphaned objects using a lifecycle policy tied to business state.

Separate upload authorization, byte transfer, and file processing. A stored object is not automatically a trusted or published document.

Check tenant ownership, allowed purpose, file limits, and the intended object namespace.

2. Use bounded transfer
Choose a streamed API path or a short-lived scoped upload URL instead of buffering arbitrary files in memory.

3. Validate completion
Confirm expected size and metadata using authoritative storage state, not a client success claim.

4. Quarantine content
Keep untrusted files separate until required validation and defensive scanning complete.

5. Process as a job
Run conversion or indexing asynchronously with resource limits and retry-safe outputs.

6. Clean abandoned objects
Expire incomplete uploads and orphaned objects using a lifecycle policy tied to business state.

The takeaway: Uploading bytes, validating content, and publishing a file are different trust boundaries.

posts.title: The Transactional Outbox / Bottleneck Roadmap
posts.headline: The Transactional Outbox
posts.hook: Updating a row and publishing an event are not one atomic operation by default.
posts.premise: A service owns relational state and must notify other systems. The outbox closes one dual-write gap, but downstream delivery can still repeat.
posts.takeaway: An outbox makes the database handoff atomic, not the entire distributed workflow exactly once.
posts.question: Which bottleneck would you measure first?

rows.detail: Choose a stable event ID, schema version, and business meaning.

rows.title: Commit state and event
rows.detail: Write the business change and outbox record in the same database transaction.

rows.title: Relay durably
rows.detail: Publish pending outbox records through a worker or supported change-data-capture path.

rows.title: Expect duplicate delivery
rows.detail: A relay can crash after publishing but before recording success.

rows.title: Deduplicate downstream effects
rows.detail: Make consumers safe for repeated event IDs and define per-entity ordering requirements.

rows.title: Manage retention and repair
rows.detail: Monitor old records, preserve replay evidence, and remove entries according to a documented policy.

posts.title: Choose the Shard Key Last / Bottleneck Roadmap
posts.headline: Choose the Shard Key Last
posts.hook: A shard key can distribute bytes evenly while concentrating every important request on one shard.
posts.premise: Consider partitioning only after measuring storage, throughput, contention, and query constraints. Distribution must fit access patterns, not just row counts.
posts.takeaway: Shard for measured access patterns, and budget for movement and cross-shard work.
posts.question: Which bottleneck would you measure first?

rows.title: Map access patterns
rows.detail: List point lookups, ranges, joins, writes, and tenant-local operations.

rows.title: Measure skew
rows.detail: Identify hot entities, time ranges, and workload imbalance before selecting a partition key.

rows.title: Choose a routing contract
rows.detail: Define how clients locate data and how routing changes during movement.

rows.title: Plan cross-shard work
rows.detail: Account for fan-out queries, distributed transactions, and global uniqueness needs.

rows.title: Design rebalancing
rows.detail: Move data with explicit ownership, consistency checks, and rollback or forward-repair rules.

rows.title: Test hotspots and growth
rows.detail: Exercise skewed traffic and a growing partition, not only uniform random keys.

posts.title: JWT Validation Is a Contract / Bottleneck Roadmap
posts.headline: JWT Validation Is a Contract
posts.hook: Decoding a token is not the same as verifying that it should be trusted.
posts.premise: A signed token is an input to a validation policy. The expected issuer, audience, algorithm, time bounds, and permission semantics must come from trusted configuration.
posts.takeaway: A valid signature is necessary for trust, but it is not the whole authorization decision.
posts.question: Which bottleneck would you measure first?

rows.title: Use a maintained validator
rows.detail: Choose a proven token-validation library rather than implementing signature rules manually.

rows.title: Pin trusted expectations
rows.detail: Configure accepted issuers, audiences, and algorithms independently of untrusted token claims.

rows.title: Verify key selection
rows.detail: Resolve signing keys through a trusted provider path with bounded caching and rotation behavior.

rows.title: Enforce time claims
rows.detail: Validate expiry and other required time bounds with a documented clock-skew policy.

rows.title: Separate permission freshness
rows.detail: Decide whether embedded permissions are current enough for the requested resource.

rows.title: Test rotation and failure
rows.detail: Exercise unknown keys, expired tokens, wrong audiences, and unavailable key discovery.

posts.headline: Authorize the Object, Not the URL
posts.hook: A hard-to-guess identifier is not an authorization policy.
posts.premise: Use two synthetic tenants and resources with clear ownership. Every read, update, export, and background operation must enforce the same boundary.
posts.takeaway: Authorization must follow the data through every direct and derived access path.
posts.question: Which bottleneck would you measure first?

rows.title: Verify tenant context
rows.detail: Derive tenant membership from trusted identity and policy, not a client-supplied tenant field alone.

rows.title: Scope data access
rows.detail: Constrain queries and resource lookups to the authorized tenant or ownership rule.

rows.title: Check each operation
rows.detail: Evaluate read, write, delete, export, and administrative permissions separately.

rows.title: Protect derived paths
rows.detail: Apply equivalent boundaries to caches, search results, files, and asynchronous jobs.

rows.title: Handle revocation
rows.detail: Define how permission changes affect sessions, cached decisions, and queued work.

rows.title: Test denied access
rows.detail: Use synthetic cross-tenant cases throughout the application surface.

posts.hook: Is 90 days enough?
posts.premise: Prepare around the actual role: problem solving, design, coding, testing, and relevant technical depth. A storage role, product backend role, and ML platform role need different specialization. Use the job description and recruiter guidance to select that depth.
posts.takeaway: Spend roughly half your time on coding and testing, one quarter on design or domain depth, and one quarter on projects, behavioral practice, and review.

rows.title: Build the mental model
rows.detail: Attempt one medium coding problem without notes, explain a previous project for ten minutes, and design a small API.

rows.title: Phase 1 / Weeks 1-3
rows.detail: Practice arrays, hashing, two pointers, sliding windows, stacks, and binary search.

rows.title: Phase 2 / Weeks 4-6
rows.detail: Add trees, graph traversal, heaps, intervals, and introductory dynamic programming.

rows.title: Phase 3 / Weeks 7-9
rows.detail: Work through a cache, notification service, file service, or other role-relevant system.

rows.title: Phase 4 / Weeks 10-12
rows.detail: Alternate unseen coding mocks, project deep dives, and design discussions. Review the actual job requirements and current recruiter instructions.

rows.title: Prove readiness
rows.detail: Recent unseen coding mocks show independent correctness and clear tests.

rows.title: Phase 4 / Weeks 5-6

rows.detail: A process and thread can be compared using resource ownership.

posts.title: Plan Your Computer Networks Preparation / Learning Roadmap
posts.headline: Plan Your Computer Networks Preparation
posts.hook: Does UDP mean packets always arrive faster?
posts.premise: Follow data from an application message to a remote service and back. Learn addresses, ports, routing, DNS, TCP/UDP, TLS, and HTTP through local experiments. Keep transport guarantees distinct from application guarantees: successful delivery of bytes does not prove a business operation completed once.
posts.takeaway: Use a local client and server you control. Predict a request trace, introduce one safe delay or disconnect, and compare the result.
posts.question: Which bottleneck would you measure first?

rows.title: Build the mental model
rows.detail: IP routes packets; transport protocols connect endpoints or deliver datagrams; TLS protects a channel; HTTP defines request semantics.

rows.title: Phase 1 / Week 1
rows.detail: Study IP addresses, subnets, routes, ports, sockets, and local versus remote destinations. Inspect your own machine's interfaces and routes.

rows.title: Phase 2 / Week 2
rows.detail: Implement a framed TCP exchange and compare it with a UDP datagram example. Test partial reads, disconnects, and timeouts.

rows.title: Phase 3 / Weeks 3-4
rows.detail: Study DNS resolution, TLS identity checks, HTTP methods, status codes, caching, and connection reuse. Compare browser timing with a command-line HTTP client.

rows.title: Phase 4 / Weeks 5-6
rows.detail: Practice slow dependencies, retry storms, proxy timeouts, resets, and DNS changes.

rows.title: Prove readiness
rows.detail: A browser request can be explained across protocol boundaries.

rows.title: Set up the scenario
rows.detail: A function opens a file, allocates a buffer, parses metadata, and may fail at any stage.

rows.title: Experiment 1
rows.detail: List resources and owners at each stage: file handle, allocated storage, parsed object, and any borrowed input.

rows.title: Experiment 2
rows.detail: Choose one cleanup strategy. In C++, wrap resources in RAII types; in C, initialize handles to safe states and route failures through ordered cleanup.

rows.title: Experiment 3
rows.detail: Inject a failure after each acquisition and test invalid metadata, empty input, and allocation failure where your harness supports it.

rows.title: Expected evidence
rows.detail: Success returns an object with an explicit ownership contract, while every failure leaves the caller without partial ownership.

rows.title: Check the result
rows.detail: Does every resource have exactly one responsible owner?

posts.title: Concurrency, Locks, and Safe Shutdown / Learning Roadmap
posts.headline: Concurrency, Locks, and Safe Shutdown
posts.hook: Does volatile make a shared counter thread-safe?
posts.premise: Concurrency is about possible interleavings and invariants, not merely adding threads. Start with the state that must remain consistent, choose a synchronization boundary, and define shutdown before optimizing throughput. A correct steady-state loop can still fail during cancellation or partial initialization.
posts.takeaway: Prefer deterministic barriers, explicit state transitions, and targeted stress tests to arbitrary sleeps.
posts.question: Which bottleneck would you measure first?

rows.title: Build the mental model
rows.detail: A lock should guard a meaningful relationship, such as queue size and contents, rather than an arbitrary line of code.

rows.title: Phase 1 / Week 1
rows.detail: Implement a shared counter and a two-field state transition.

rows.title: Phase 2 / Week 2
rows.detail: Build a bounded queue with not-empty and not-full predicates. Handle multiple producers and consumers.

rows.title: Phase 3 / Week 3
rows.detail: Add explicit closing state and decide whether queued work drains or is cancelled.

rows.title: Phase 4 / Week 4
rows.detail: Measure lock hold time, throughput, and tail latency. Compare smaller critical sections, partitioned state, and batching before changing primitives.

rows.title: Prove readiness
rows.detail: Each lock has a stated invariant and ownership rule.

posts.premise: Concurrency is about possible interleavings and invariants, not merely adding threads. Start with the state that must remain consistent, choose a synchronization boundary, and define shutdown before optimizing throughput. A correct steady-state loop can still fail during cancellation or partial initialization.
posts.takeaway: Prefer deterministic barriers, explicit state transitions, and targeted stress tests to arbitrary sleeps.
posts.question: How would you reproduce this with synthetic data?

rows.title: Set up the scenario
rows.detail: Several producers submit tasks to a capacity-limited queue and workers process them.

rows.title: Experiment 1
rows.detail: Under one lock, set a closing flag and stop accepting new submissions.

rows.title: Experiment 2
rows.detail: Notify waiting producers so they can observe closure. Workers wait while the queue is empty and not closing; when closing and empty, they exit.

rows.title: Experiment 3
rows.detail: Join all workers before freeing queue storage or callbacks they use.

rows.title: Expected evidence
rows.detail: The drain policy gives every accepted item a terminal outcome, and all waiters have an exit condition. Shared memory remains alive until workers stop referencing it.

rows.title: Check the result
rows.detail: Does close wake producers as well as consumers?

posts.headline: Databases, SQL, Indexes, and Transactions
posts.hook: Why not put an index on every column?
posts.premise: A database is not just a place to store JSON. Its schema and transaction boundaries encode invariants, while indexes trade read efficiency for write and storage cost. Learn these decisions using a small order or reservation model and inspect actual query behavior.
posts.takeaway: Use PostgreSQL or another well-documented local database and synthetic data. Write the expected rows before running a query.
posts.question: Which bottleneck would you measure first?

rows.title: Build the mental model
rows.detail: Know what one row represents in every table and intermediate result. Joining multiple one-to-many relationships can multiply rows.

rows.title: Phase 1 / Week 1
rows.detail: Build customers, orders, and items with primary and foreign keys. Practice joins, grouping, NULL behavior, and window functions.

rows.title: Phase 2 / Week 2
rows.detail: Create a larger synthetic dataset and inspect query plans. Compare selective lookups, ordered history, and broad scans.

rows.title: Phase 3 / Week 3
rows.detail: Use two sessions to reproduce a lost update or last-item reservation race. Add the database-enforced invariant and choose an appropriate transaction strategy.

rows.title: Phase 4 / Week 4
rows.detail: Practice a backward-compatible schema change, migration rollback or forward repair, backup, and restore in a disposable database.

rows.title: Prove readiness
rows.detail: Schema keys and output grain are explicit.

posts.headline: Trace a Request Through DNS, TLS, and HTTP
posts.hook: Does HTTPS mean a site is trustworthy?
posts.premise: A browser request involves naming, connection selection, transport, server identity, HTTP semantics, intermediaries, and response rendering. The exact path depends on caches, existing connections, protocol versions, and proxies. Explain a concrete request rather than a memorized universal sequence.
posts.takeaway: Choose one public page and one local API you control. Record the protocol and timing for each observation.
posts.question: Which bottleneck would you measure first?

rows.title: Build the mental model
rows.detail: DNS maps names to records, often through caches with TTLs. A successful lookup does not prove the endpoint is reachable or healthy.

rows.title: Phase 1 / Days 1-3
rows.detail: Inspect the URL components, DNS records, cache behavior, and destination port.

rows.title: Phase 2 / Days 4-6
rows.detail: Study TCP versus QUIC at the level needed to explain setup, loss, and streams. Inspect a valid certificate chain and hostname.

rows.title: Phase 3 / Days 7-10
rows.detail: Implement a local endpoint with status codes, cache headers, and conditional requests. Observe redirects, request bodies, and response headers.

rows.title: Phase 4 / Days 11-14
rows.detail: Measure DNS, connection, TLS, server wait, and transfer time where the tool exposes them. Add a controlled server delay and a larger payload separately.

rows.title: Prove readiness
rows.detail: One real request can be explained with observed protocol details.

rows.detail: Remove flaky assumptions, keep test fixtures deterministic, and record why a check exists. Review dependency updates and permissions.

posts.title: Distributed Systems from First Principles / Learning Roadmap
posts.headline: Distributed Systems from First Principles
posts.hook: Does replication guarantee no data loss?
posts.premise: A distributed system contains independently failing components that communicate with uncertain delays. Correct design states what remains true during retries, crashes, and partitions. Start from invariants and failure boundaries, then select replication and coordination mechanisms that support the promised behavior.
posts.takeaway: For every design, trace success, lost response, duplicate delivery, process crash, and partition.
posts.question: Which bottleneck would you measure first?

rows.title: Build the mental model
rows.detail: The remote operation may not have started, may still be running, or may have completed with a lost response. The client cannot infer which solely from elapsed time.

rows.title: Phase 1 / Week 1
rows.detail: Study RPC timeouts, retries, idempotency keys, backoff, and deadlines. Build a request table that stores a logical operation's status and result.

rows.title: Phase 2 / Week 2
rows.detail: Compare leader-based replication, asynchronous replicas, and quorum concepts. Describe stale reads and failover behavior.

rows.title: Phase 3 / Weeks 3-4
rows.detail: Study logs, consensus at a conceptual level, leases, epochs, and fencing. Analyze a paused worker that resumes after replacement.

rows.title: Phase 4 / Weeks 5-6
rows.detail: Add bounded queues, backpressure, observability, and failure injection. Define service-level goals, recovery objectives, and a runbook.

rows.title: Prove readiness
rows.detail: Every important operation has a named invariant.

rows.title: Set up the scenario
rows.detail: A worker updates a database and crashes before acknowledging its queue message. The broker later redelivers the same job.

rows.title: Experiment 1
rows.detail: Give the job a stable ID. In the same database transaction as the business update, record that the job has been applied, using a uniqueness constraint.

rows.title: Experiment 2
rows.detail: On redelivery, inspect the durable job record and return the stored outcome rather than repeating the effect.

rows.title: Experiment 3
rows.detail: If the effect is an external API call rather than a local transaction, preserve a provider idempotency key and reconcile ambiguous outcomes.

rows.title: Expected evidence
rows.detail: The local database effect is deduplicated under the stated transaction contract.

rows.title: Check the result
rows.detail: Is the deduplication record committed with the local effect?

posts.title: Plan Your DSA Preparation in Eight Weeks / Learning Roadmap
posts.headline: Plan Your DSA Preparation in Eight Weeks
posts.hook: Should I finish one topic completely before moving on?
posts.premise: Study data structures through the operations they support and algorithms through the invariants that make them correct. Use topic-focused practice to learn, then mixed unseen problems to test recognition. A complete preparation loop includes clarification, implementation, testing, complexity, and revision.
posts.takeaway: Use three focused problem sessions, one review session, and one mixed mock each week. Re-solve failures from a blank editor after a delay.
posts.question: Which bottleneck would you measure first?

rows.title: Build the mental model
rows.detail: Input size, ordering, value range, mutation rules, and output requirements change the solution.

rows.title: Phase 1 / Weeks 1-2
rows.detail: Cover arrays, maps, sets, pointers, windows, stacks, and binary search. Trace indexes and counts explicitly.

rows.title: Phase 2 / Weeks 3-4
rows.detail: Study recursion, iterative traversal, BFS, DFS, priority queues, connected components, and topological order.

rows.title: Phase 3 / Weeks 5-6
rows.detail: Practice backtracking, greedy arguments, intervals, and dynamic programming.

rows.title: Phase 4 / Weeks 7-8
rows.detail: Use unseen mixed sets and realistic time limits. Preserve time for tests and complexity.

rows.title: Prove readiness
rows.detail: Mixed unseen problems can be approached without category hints.

posts.hook: When is sorting better than hashing?
posts.premise: Arrays give indexed access and locality; hashing trades memory for keyed lookup; two pointers exploit ordering or a maintained partition. The useful skill is recognizing which information must be retained and which candidate region can be discarded safely.
posts.takeaway: For each exercise, write the required output and duplicate policy first. Solve a small baseline, then explain what the map or pointer invariant eliminates.
posts.question: Which bottleneck would you measure first?

rows.title: Build the mental model
rows.detail: A problem may ask for original indexes, unique values, or all valid pairs. Sorting can destroy original positional information unless it is retained.

rows.title: Phase 1 / Days 1-3
rows.detail: Practice traversal, stable compaction, prefix/suffix accumulation, and in-place updates.

rows.title: Phase 2 / Days 4-6
rows.detail: Study complement lookup, duplicates, anagrams, and frequency grouping. Decide whether the map stores a count, earliest index, latest index, or a list of positions.

rows.title: Phase 3 / Days 7-10
rows.detail: Practice pair sums, deduplicated triples, and merging sorted sequences. Justify each pointer movement and where duplicates should be skipped.

rows.title: Phase 4 / Days 11-14
rows.detail: Change one requirement at a time: return counts, preserve order, forbid mutation, or allow repeated results.

rows.title: Prove readiness
rows.detail: The map value's meaning is explicit.

rows.title: Set up the scenario
rows.detail: With unlimited positive coin values 1 and 2, count ways to make amount 3 when order does not matter.

rows.detail: Explain the alternative loop order: iterating target amounts outside and choosing the last coin inside counts ordered sequences, so 1+2 and 2+1 become different.

posts.headline: Heaps, Intervals, and Greedy Proofs
posts.hook: Is the heap array sorted?
posts.premise: Heaps maintain an extreme under updates, interval problems depend on endpoint semantics, and greedy algorithms need a proof that a local choice preserves an optimal solution. These tools often combine in scheduling and streaming problems, but each solves a different part of the reasoning.
posts.takeaway: Write a tiny counterexample to a tempting incorrect rule, such as choosing the shortest or highest-profit interval.
posts.question: Which bottleneck would you measure first?

rows.title: Build the mental model
rows.detail: A min-heap gives the smallest element efficiently, but does not keep every element in sorted order for arbitrary queries.

rows.title: Phase 1 / Sessions 1-3
rows.detail: Practice insertion, extraction, bounded top-k, and merging sorted streams.

rows.title: Phase 2 / Sessions 4-6
rows.detail: Solve merging, overlap detection, room allocation, and removal-count variants. Sort on the field needed by the proof, not automatically by start.

rows.title: Phase 3 / Sessions 7-10
rows.detail: Study earliest-finish scheduling, reachable-range expansion, and monotone choices. Explain an exchange or dominance argument.

rows.title: Phase 4 / Sessions 11-14
rows.detail: Combine heaps with offline sorting, query processing, or multiple streams. Remove expired or stale heap entries as required.

rows.title: Prove readiness
rows.detail: Heap entries and their priority have explicit meanings.

posts.title: Binary Search, Sorting, and Boundary Proofs / Learning Roadmap
posts.headline: Binary Search, Sorting, and Boundary Proofs
posts.hook: Why does binary search sometimes loop forever?
posts.premise: Binary search finds a boundary in an ordered or monotone search space. Its correctness depends on the meaning of the bounds and the update rule. Sorting creates useful order but has its own cost, stability, and memory implications. Learn both as reasoning tools rather than syntax patterns.
posts.takeaway: Use one clear lower-bound implementation until its invariant is natural. Draw the retained interval after each comparison.
posts.question: Which bottleneck would you measure first?

rows.title: Build the mental model
rows.detail: A lower bound is the first position whose value is at least the target; an upper bound is the first position greater than it.

rows.title: Phase 1 / Sessions 1-3
rows.detail: Implement exact search and lower bound with half-open intervals. Test empty input, one element, target below all values, target above all values, and duplicates.

rows.title: Phase 2 / Sessions 4-5
rows.detail: Use lower and upper bounds to find a target range or count occurrences. Preserve original indexes if sorting is introduced.

rows.title: Phase 3 / Sessions 6-8
rows.detail: Practice minimum capacity or speed with a monotone feasibility check.

rows.title: Phase 4 / Sessions 9-10
rows.detail: Compare sorting with hashing and selection. Discuss stable order, comparator consistency, worst-case versus expected bounds, and output requirements.

rows.title: Prove readiness
rows.detail: The search invariant and termination argument are explicit.

posts.title: Plan Your System Design Preparation / Learning Roadmap
posts.headline: Plan Your System Design Preparation
posts.hook: How much capacity math should I do?
posts.premise: System design is a structured discussion of requirements, data, interfaces, capacity, and failure. Start with a small correct design, identify the important bottlenecks, and deepen only the parts that matter. A defensible trade-off is more valuable than a diagram containing every fashionable component.
posts.takeaway: For every practice design, write a one-page contract before drawing. Use the same delivery structure, but choose deep dives from the problem.
posts.question: Which bottleneck would you measure first?

rows.title: Build the mental model
rows.detail: Ask who uses the system, which operations matter, what scale is assumed, and what correctness or latency is required.

rows.title: Phase 1 / Weeks 1-2
rows.detail: Review APIs, SQL/NoSQL access patterns, indexes, HTTP, caching, replication, and queues. Design a small link or task service with explicit data ownership and errors.

rows.title: Phase 2 / Week 3
rows.detail: Practice idempotency, transactions, consistency, leases, and authorization. Trace timeouts and partial failures.

rows.title: Phase 3 / Weeks 4-5
rows.detail: Study partitioning, hot keys, fan-out, backpressure, large objects, and regional failure. Add observability and capacity budgets.

rows.title: Phase 4 / Week 6
rows.detail: Run timed design discussions with a peer who changes one constraint. Practice explaining rejected alternatives and uncertainty.

rows.title: Prove readiness
rows.detail: Requirements and non-goals are prioritized.

rows.title: Set up the scenario
rows.detail: Assume 20 million requests/day, a 10x peak factor, 200 ms mean time in system at peak, and 1 KB of durable event data per request.

rows.title: Experiment 1
rows.detail: Compute average load: 20,000,000 / 86,400 is about 231 requests/second. A 10x illustrative peak is about 2,315 requests/second.

rows.title: Experiment 2
rows.detail: Using L = lambda times W under the relevant steady-state assumptions, about 2,315 * 0.2 gives 463 requests in the system on average at that load.

rows.title: Experiment 3
rows.detail: At decimal 1 KB per event, raw growth is about 20 GB/day. Thirty days is about 600 GB before replication, indexes, metadata, and compression.

rows.title: Expected evidence
rows.detail: The calculation supplies approximate rate, concurrency, and storage dimensions with clear assumptions.

rows.detail: Are decimal and binary storage units labeled consistently?

posts.title: Caching and Database Scaling Without Stale Promises / Learning Roadmap
posts.headline: Caching and Database Scaling Without Stale Promises
posts.hook: Does a high hit ratio prove the cache is successful?
posts.premise: A cache stores a reusable result under an eligibility and freshness policy. It is not automatically an authoritative source. Replicas and partitions address different scaling needs, and every optimization changes the failure path. Start with measured access patterns and explicit staleness tolerance.
posts.takeaway: Add a cache only after measuring a repeatable expensive read. Document the source of truth, cache key, expiration, invalidation, and fallback.
posts.question: Which bottleneck would you measure first?

rows.title: Build the mental model
rows.detail: Include every input that affects the result, such as tenant, user scope, query, version, or locale where relevant.

rows.title: Phase 1 / Week 1
rows.detail: Implement cache-aside for a safe read and measure hit rate, miss latency, and backend load. Define positive and negative caching separately.

rows.title: Phase 2 / Week 2, first half
rows.detail: Simulate many misses for one key and add request coalescing or bounded refresh. Consider jittered expiry and stale serving only where allowed.

rows.title: Phase 3 / Week 2, second half
rows.detail: Compare read replicas, vertical changes, and sharding against the actual workload. Describe lag, routing, hot partitions, and transaction boundaries.

rows.title: Phase 4 / Week 3
rows.detail: Remove the cache or delay a replica in a local test. Apply backpressure, admission limits, and safe fallbacks.

rows.title: Prove readiness
rows.detail: Source of truth and cache eligibility are explicit.

posts.title: File Storage, Sync, and Snapshot Design / Learning Roadmap
posts.headline: File Storage, Sync, and Snapshot Design
posts.hook: Is a snapshot always application-consistent?
posts.premise: Separate durable data bytes from metadata that names and authorizes them. Large-file systems need partial-upload handling, immutable versions, conflict rules, and garbage collection that never removes live data. A fast happy-path upload is not enough to establish durability or safe multi-device behavior.
posts.takeaway: Use small synthetic files and a local object directory plus a metadata database. Simulate interrupted uploads and conflicting versions.
posts.question: Which bottleneck would you measure first?

rows.title: Build the mental model
rows.detail: Upload chunks or parts first, validate them, and publish a complete manifest through an authoritative metadata operation.

rows.title: Phase 1 / Week 1
rows.detail: Define upload IDs, part checksums, ownership, completion, expiry, and file manifests. Add an expected-base-version condition to metadata changes.

rows.title: Phase 2 / Week 2, first half
rows.detail: Model per-device cursors and an ordered change log. Test rename, offline edit, duplicate completion, and deletion.

rows.title: Phase 3 / Week 2, second half
rows.detail: Represent a snapshot as an immutable reference to a versioned manifest or mapping root. Use copy-on-write for later changes.

rows.title: Phase 4 / Week 3
rows.detail: Add orphan-upload cleanup, checksum validation, corruption reporting, and safe reference-based reclamation. Estimate metadata and changed-data growth separately.

rows.title: Prove readiness
rows.detail: Upload, commit, and visibility boundaries are distinct.

rows.title: Set up the scenario
rows.detail: A client uploads a file as three chunks and then sends a completion request. The last chunk upload succeeds, but the completion response is lost.

rows.title: Experiment 1
rows.detail: Assign an upload ID and expected file base version. Store verified chunk identities and checksums without marking the file version current.

rows.title: Experiment 2
rows.detail: Atomically commit a manifest referencing all three chunks and record the completion operation result.

rows.title: Experiment 3
rows.detail: Publish the change-log entry with the metadata transaction or through a reliable outbox. The second device reads a complete manifest and can fetch chunks.

rows.title: Expected evidence
rows.detail: The new version is either absent or fully committed from a reader's perspective.

rows.title: Check the result
rows.detail: Can a manifest reference a missing or unverified chunk?

posts.headline: API Design, Authentication, and Authorization
posts.hook: Is authentication enough to secure an API?
posts.premise: A good API defines behavior under valid requests, invalid input, retries, and unauthorized access. Authentication establishes identity; authorization decides permitted actions on a resource. Neither a signed token nor a hidden frontend control automatically enforces object-level access.
posts.takeaway: Use a local service and synthetic users with different permissions. Write authorization tests before adding UI controls.
posts.question: Which bottleneck would you measure first?

rows.title: Build the mental model
rows.detail: A client-supplied role, price, tenant ID, or paid flag is input to validate, not authority.

rows.title: Phase 1 / Week 1
rows.detail: Define resources, methods, errors, required fields, size limits, and stable pagination. Validate types and business constraints.

rows.title: Phase 2 / Week 2, first half
rows.detail: Integrate an established authentication approach in a test environment. Understand token verification, session expiry, secure transport, and secret storage.

rows.title: Phase 3 / Week 2, second half
rows.detail: Test two users and two tenants accessing each other's objects. Apply authorization to reads, writes, downloads, and background operations.

rows.title: Phase 4 / Week 3
rows.detail: Add payload-bound idempotency for selected writes, rate and size limits, safe errors, and audit metadata. Review dependency failure and partial completion.

rows.title: Prove readiness
rows.detail: Identity and resource permissions are separate and tested.

posts.title: Observability, Reliability, and Incident Response / Learning Roadmap
posts.headline: Observability, Reliability, and Incident Response
posts.hook: Are more logs always better?
posts.premise: Observability helps answer questions about system behavior; reliability connects that behavior to user needs. Metrics, logs, and traces are complementary evidence. A useful incident process prioritizes mitigation, clear coordination, and later learning without substituting blame or dashboards for a tested recovery plan.
posts.takeaway: Practice only on a local or approved test service. Write a small runbook, inject a reversible failure, and have a peer follow the instructions.
posts.question: Which bottleneck would you measure first?

rows.title: Build the mental model
rows.detail: Availability should describe successful useful work, not merely an open port. Latency objectives need a population and percentile or threshold definition.

rows.title: Phase 1 / Week 1
rows.detail: Choose one user journey and define success, latency, and acceptable errors. Instrument request count, duration, failure, dependency time, and saturation.

rows.title: Phase 2 / Week 2, first half
rows.detail: Create an alert for sustained user impact with an owner and response action. Use traces or correlated logs to separate application work from dependency delay.

rows.title: Phase 3 / Week 2, second half
rows.detail: Introduce a slow local dependency, exhausted connection pool, or bad configuration. Record detection time, hypotheses, mitigation, and validation.

rows.title: Phase 4 / Week 3
rows.detail: Write a blameless review covering impact, contributing factors, what worked, and specific follow-ups. Assign owners and validation criteria.

rows.title: Prove readiness
rows.detail: Indicators reflect a defined user journey.

posts.headline: AI-Assisted Coding with Tests and Review
posts.hook: Should I accept code I cannot explain?
posts.premise: Use the assistant to propose, explain, and implement bounded changes while the specification and tests define success. Start from the controlling code path, make a small change, and run the cheapest check that could prove the hypothesis wrong. Human review remains essential for security, compatibility, and intent.
posts.takeaway: Use a small personal repository and an existing failing test. Compare assisted and manual work on similar tasks, including review time.
posts.question: Which bottleneck would you measure first?

rows.title: Build the mental model
rows.detail: Name the failing behavior, relevant file or API, constraints, and expected result. Ask for the smallest change that tests a local hypothesis.

rows.title: Phase 1 / Days 1-3
rows.detail: Choose a small bug or feature. Write the current behavior, intended contract, non-goals, and a focused check.

rows.title: Phase 2 / Days 4-6
rows.detail: Ask the assistant to identify the controlling code and propose a minimal patch. Run a behavior-scoped test immediately after the change.

rows.title: Phase 3 / Days 7-10
rows.detail: Inspect edge cases, error paths, dependencies, public APIs, and security boundaries. Verify unfamiliar API claims against documentation.

rows.title: Phase 4 / Days 11-14
rows.detail: Record elapsed time including review, defects found, and rework. Keep the helpful task patterns and remove unreliable shortcuts.

rows.title: Prove readiness
rows.detail: Task scope and acceptance criteria are explicit.

posts.hook: Can equal-dimensional embeddings from different models be mixed?

Retrieval quality depends on candidate coverage, filters, indexing, ranking, and evaluation. Compare with lexical and exact-match baselines, especially for identifiers and specialized vocabulary.

posts.headline: SQL and Analytics Interview Practice
posts.hook: Why can NOT IN behave unexpectedly with NULL?
posts.premise: SQL interview quality depends on the data contract as much as syntax. Define row grain, keys, timezone, ties, and missing-value meaning before choosing joins or windows. Use small hand-checkable datasets and adversarial fixtures to verify results rather than trusting a query because it executes.
posts.takeaway: Write the expected result for a tiny dataset before writing SQL. Include duplicates, ties, unmatched rows, NULLs, and immature time windows.
posts.question: Which bottleneck would you measure first?

rows.title: Build the mental model
rows.detail: State what each input and output row represents. Joining two child tables can multiply records before SUM or COUNT executes.

rows.title: Phase 1 / Days 1-3
rows.detail: Practice inner and left joins, aggregation, anti-joins, and NULL behavior. Build customers, orders, and payments with deliberate duplicate and missing relationships.

rows.title: Phase 2 / Days 4-6
rows.detail: Practice top-N per group, latest-record deduplication, running totals, and gaps-and-islands. Define ties and stable secondary keys.

rows.title: Phase 3 / Days 7-10
rows.detail: Define cohorts, day-based retention, ordered funnels, and rolling windows.

rows.title: Phase 4 / Days 11-14
rows.detail: Inspect plans on a larger synthetic dataset, add justified indexes, and compare results before and after optimization.

rows.title: Prove readiness
rows.detail: Input and output grain are explicit.

posts.title: Explain Technical Work Clearly / Learning Roadmap
posts.headline: Explain Technical Work Clearly
posts.hook: How short should a technical summary be?
posts.premise: Good technical communication helps someone make a decision or reproduce a result. Start with the audience and question, separate facts from hypotheses, and choose the smallest structure that preserves the important reasoning. A concise explanation can still include assumptions, evidence, and limitations.
posts.takeaway: Take one real but shareable technical task and explain it in three forms: one sentence, a short review summary, and a deeper note.
posts.question: Which bottleneck would you measure first?

rows.title: Build the mental model
rows.detail: A reviewer needs to know what changed and why before reading implementation detail. A stakeholder needs impact and next action. An interviewer needs your reasoning.

rows.title: Phase 1 / Days 1-3
rows.detail: Practice writing expected behavior, actual behavior, impact, environment, and a minimal reproducer. Remove irrelevant chronology and unsupported cause claims.

rows.title: Phase 2 / Days 4-6
rows.detail: Write a short note with requirements, constraints, two alternatives, chosen approach, and consequences.

rows.title: Phase 3 / Days 7-10
rows.detail: Practice status updates that distinguish completed, verified, blocked, and next work. Summarize a patch through behavior and risk.

rows.title: Phase 4 / Days 11-14
rows.detail: Rehearse a project walkthrough with interruptions. Define unfamiliar terms, pause for clarifying questions, and answer the question asked before adding detail.

rows.title: Prove readiness
rows.detail: The audience's question is answered early.
